lessons.readme:
# Refresher: A Whole Program

**The idea: every C++ program starts running at `main`.**

Like a recipe card. The top lists what you need. The steps start at one place.

```cpp
#include <iostream>          // bring in the printing tools

int main() {
    int beds = 4;            // a variable: a type, a name, a value
    std::cout << "beds: " << beds << std::endl;
    return 0;                // 0 means "finished fine"
}
```

- `#include` copies in a library's declarations.
- `std::cout <<` prints. `std::endl` ends the line.
- `std::` means "from the standard library".

This prints `beds: 4`.

**Check:** where does the program start?

questions.question: Where does a C++ program start running?
answers: At the first function in the file
At the last line of the file

questions.question: What does `std::cout << "hi" << std::endl;` do?
answers: Prints hi, then ends the line
Reads hi from the keyboard into a variable
questions.answer: Prints hi, then ends the line

questions.question: Remember (Start Here): what can you bring into the final?
answers: Printed lecture slides and your lab code

# Refresher: Writing Functions

**The idea: a function is a named, reusable job. Values go in, one value comes out.**

Like a vending machine: you put in a code, you get one snack.

```cpp
int maxOf(int a, int b) {   // return type, name, parameters
    if (a > b) return a;
    return b;
}

int big = maxOf(3, 8);       // big is 8
```

- The type before the name is what it **returns**. `void` means nothing.
- `return` hands the value back and leaves the function right away.

## Assignment

Complete both functions in `basics.h`.

1. [ ] `maxOf(a, b)`: return the bigger of the two.
2. [ ] `sumTo(n)`: return 1 + 2 + ... + n with a `for` loop. `sumTo(0)` is 0.

lessons.title: Refresher: Reference Parameters
lessons.readme:
# Refresher: Reference Parameters

**The idea: a `&` on a parameter means "work on the caller's own variable, not a copy".**

Like lending a friend your notebook vs handing them a photocopy. Writing in the notebook changes yours.

```cpp
void addOne(int& n) {   // & : n IS the caller's variable
    n = n + 1;
}

int beds = 4;
addOne(beds);           // beds is now 5
```

Without the `&`, `n` would be a copy. `beds` would stay 4.

`const int& n` means "use mine, but don't change it". It skips the copy for big things like vectors.

> [!note]
> The Pointers and Memory chapter covers references fully. This is enough to read the code before then.

**Check:** what is `beds` after the call?

questions.question: `void addOne(int& n) { n = n + 1; }` is called as `addOne(beds)` with `beds = 4`. What is `beds` after?
Same function, but written `void addOne(int n)`. What is `beds` after?
Remember: what does `return` do?
answers: Prints the value to the screen, then keeps going
Ends the whole program right away
Hands back a value and leaves the function
Restarts the function from the top
questions.answer: Hands back a value and leaves the function

lessons.title: Refresher: std::vector
lessons.readme:
# Refresher: std::vector

**The idea: a `vector` is an array that grows when you add to it.**

Like a train that adds a car whenever you need room.

```cpp
vector<int> v;          // empty
v.push_back(7);         // {7}
v.push_back(2);         // {7, 2}
int first = v[0];       // 7
int n = v.size();       // 2
```

- `v[i]` reads slot `i`. Slots start at 0.
- `v.size()` is how many items are in it.
- Pass it as `const vector<int>&` to avoid copying it.

## Assignment

Complete both functions in `basics.h`.

1. [ ] `total(v)`: return the sum of every item. An empty vector sums to 0.
2. [ ] `evens(v)`: return a new vector of only the even items, in the same order.

lessons.title: Refresher: new, delete and the Arrow
lessons.readme:
# Refresher: new, delete and the Arrow

**The idea: `new` builds something that outlives the function. You get back its address.**

Like renting a storage unit. It stays until you give it back. You keep the unit number.

```cpp
Drink* d = new Drink();   // build it; d holds its address
d->size = 16;             // -> : "go to that address, then use .size"
delete d;                 // give the unit back
```

- `d->size` is short for `(*d).size`.
- Every `new` needs one `delete`. Forget it and you **leak** memory.
- A plain `Drink d;` disappears when the function ends.

> [!note]
> The Pointers and Memory chapter explains addresses fully. For now: `new` gives an address, `->` reaches through it.

**Check:** what does every `new` need?

questions.question: What does every `new` need?
answers: Nothing, it is freed for you

questions.question: `d` holds the address of a `Drink`. How do you read its `size`?
Remember: what does `v.size()` give for a `vector`?
answers: The index of the last item plus one byte

lessons.readme:
# Refresher: Templates

**The idea: a template is code with a blank for the type. You fill in the blank when you use it.**

Like a cookie cutter. Same shape, any dough.

```cpp
template <typename T>
T biggest(T a, T b) {
    if (a > b) return a;
    return b;
}

biggest(3, 8);          // T is int
biggest(2.5, 1.0);      // T is double
```

You've already used one: `vector<int>` is the `vector` template with `T = int`.

Later chapters build containers this way, like `Stack<T>` or a `Node<T>` that holds any type.

**Check:** what is `T` in `vector<int>`?

questions.question: In `vector<int>`, what fills the template's type blank?
`template <typename T> T biggest(T a, T b)` is called as `biggest(2.5, 1.0)`. What is `T`?
Remember: what does `d->size` mean?
answers: Delete `d`, then read whatever its `size` was
Go to the address in `d`, then read `size`
questions.answer: Go to the address in `d`, then read `size`

lessons.title: Classes and Objects
lessons.readme:
# Classes and Objects

**The idea: a class bundles data with the functions that use it.**

![a glass of pearl milk tea with dark tapioca pearls at the bottom](courses/diagrams/e1e9c215-66b6-55eb-8d65-fc8d064efe01/bubble-tea.jpg)
*Image: Battlesnake1, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.*

The lecture builds a boba cafe simulator. One order visits four stations. A `Drink` gets passed along, and each station fills in one part:

![a drink passes through the kiosk, brewer, cooker and topping station](courses/diagrams/e1e9c215-66b6-55eb-8d65-fc8d064efe01/flow.svg)

There are three ways to organize code like this:

- **Procedural:** a list of steps (C works this way).
- **Functional:** functions with inputs and outputs, no side effects.
- **Object-oriented (OOP):** objects that hold data plus the functions for that data.

C++ lets you do OOP, but doesn't force it.

**Check:** which style uses functions with no side effects?

questions.question: Which style breaks a program into functions that have **no side effects**?
Which style organizes a program as objects that hold data and the functions for that data?

lessons.title: Public, Private and Structs
lessons.readme:
# Public, Private and Structs

**The idea: outside code can only use the public part. That hiding is called encapsulation.**

Think of a vending machine. You press buttons (public). You can't reach the gears inside (private).

**Encapsulation** = data and functions together, behind an interface. The cafe can swap out its cooker, and code that calls `doOrder` doesn't change.

A `struct` is the same as a class with **one** difference:

| | starts out |
|---|---|
| `class` | private |
| `struct` | **public** |

Use a struct for a plain bag of data (like `Drink`). Use a class when there's behavior and something to hide.

**Check:** what's the default access in a struct?

lessons.title: Constructors and Init Lists
lessons.readme:
# Constructors and Init Lists

**The idea: a constructor sets up a new object so it never starts with garbage.**

It has the class's name and **no return type**. The part after the colon is the **initializer list**. It runs **before** the body.

```cpp
BobaCafe() : num_drinks_served(0) {
    std::cout << "Boba Cafe Initialized." << std::endl;
}
```

![memory, then the init list, then the constructor body](courses/diagrams/0c914b6b-4e70-53ca-b6fe-b15981a27111/steps.svg)

By the time the body runs, members already exist. So three kinds of members **must** go in the list:

- a `const` member
- a reference member
- a member whose class has no no-argument constructor

> [!warning]
> Once you write **any** constructor, the free `Class()` one disappears. Members are set in the order they're **declared**, not the order you list them.

## Assignment

Give the cafe a cooker that starts out full.

1. [ ] Give `BobaCooker(int capacity)` an init list: set `capacity`, start `servings_left` at that capacity, and `refill_count` at 0.
2. [ ] Give `BobaCafe()` an init list: build `bobaCooker` with capacity 3, and start `num_drinks_served` at 0.

It won't compile until you do. The error names the two members that must be in a list.

# Static and Const Members

**The idea: a static member is one variable shared by every object of the class.**

Like the class whiteboard. Every student has their own notebook. There's only one whiteboard, and everyone sees the same thing on it.

"How many cafes are open?" isn't about one cafe. So it's static:

![two cafes with their own ids sharing one static counter](courses/diagrams/d5404960-7481-5543-88b0-94907e1aa0c6/shared.svg)

```cpp
class BobaCafe {
    static int num_open;          // one copy for the whole class
    int num_drinks_served;        // one copy per cafe
};
int BobaCafe::num_open = 0;       // defined once, outside, no 'static'
```

Make ten cafes: still one `num_open`.

**Check:** trace the lockers below.

questions.question: A class has `static int count;` and you create 5 objects. How many `count` variables exist?

lessons.title: Static Functions Have No this
lessons.readme:
# Static Functions Have No this

**The idea: a static function belongs to the class, not to any one object.**

You call it with no object: `BobaCafe::getNumOpen()`.

So it has **no `this`** (the pointer to "the object I was called on"). That means it can only use static members.

```cpp
static int getNumOpen() { return num_open; }   // fine: num_open is static
```

**Check:** can a static function read `num_drinks_served` (a normal member)?

questions.question: A `static` member function can:
answers: Be called only on an existing object
Use any member of the class through `this`
Use static members, but has no `this`
questions.answer: Use static members, but has no `this`

questions.question: Why can't a static member function use a normal (non-static) data member?
answers: It has no `this`, so there is no object to read from
It can, as long as the function itself is marked const
Static functions cannot read any variables
questions.answer: It has no `this`, so there is no object to read from

lessons.title: Const Member Functions
lessons.readme:
# Const Member Functions

**The idea: a `const` after a method's parentheses promises it won't change the object.**

```cpp
int served() const { return num_drinks_served; }   // reads, never writes
```

It can't change normal members. It **can** change static ones, because those aren't part of the object.

`const` means something different in each spot:

```cpp
const string& foo(const string& arg) const;
//  1st: caller can't change what's returned
//  2nd: foo can't change arg
//  3rd: foo can't change *this
```

**Check:** which line is allowed inside a const method?

questions.question: Remember (Setters That Say No): a setter rejects a value. What happens to the member?

lessons.title: Destructors
lessons.readme:
# Destructors

**The idea: a destructor cleans up when an object dies. It runs by itself.**

```cpp
~BobaCafe() {
    std::cout << "Number of drinks served: " << num_drinks_served << std::endl;
}
```

`~` + class name. **No parameters, no return type, only one per class.** You never call it yourself. It runs:

- for a local object: when it **goes out of scope** (hits its closing `}`)
- for an object made with `new`: when you **`delete`** it

Locals die in **reverse** order of creation:

![two cafes constructed and destroyed as their scopes end](courses/diagrams/733bb6c8-4f3b-58c8-8c14-09bd1e430438/life.svg)

## Assignment

Track every cafe with the static members.

1. [ ] In the constructor, add 1 to `num_open`.
2. [ ] In the destructor, subtract 1 from `num_open`, and add this cafe's `num_drinks_served` to `total_served`.
3. [ ] Complete the static functions `getNumOpen()` and `getTotalServed()`.

lessons.title: Writing a Constructor and Destructor
lessons.readme:
# Writing a Constructor and Destructor

**The idea: memorize this shape. Quizzes ask you to write both from scratch.**

```cpp
class Kettle {
    double liters;
public:
    Kettle(double l) : liters(l) {}                               // constructor
    ~Kettle() { std::cout << "Kettle cooled." << std::endl; }    // destructor
};
```

**Constructor checklist:**
- Name = class name. No return type, not even `void`.
- Parameter type matches the member (`double`, not `int`).
- After the colon: `member(parameter)`. No `=`.
- Still needs a body: `{}`.

**Destructor checklist:**
- `~` + class name + empty `()`.
- No init list.
- "Prints" means `std::cout << ... << std::endl;`.

> [!warning]
> Copy the message exactly, including the period.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Write `Speaker`'s constructor: it takes the volume as a `double` and sets `volume` in an init list.
2. [ ] Write the destructor: it prints `Speaker off.` followed by `std::endl`.

It won't compile until the constructor exists.

lessons.title: Headers and Separate Compilation
lessons.readme:
# Headers and Separate Compilation

**The idea: split code into files so one small edit only rebuilds one file.**

- **Header (`.h`):** declarations. The "what".
- **Source (`.cpp`):** definitions. The "how".

Each `.cpp` compiles alone into an object file. The **linker** joins them into one program:

![two source files compiled separately, then linked](courses/diagrams/306c2ad6-54e8-5851-935e-3c5ffb59b65e/build.svg)

Edit one line in `teabrewer.cpp`. Only that file recompiles, then everything relinks:

![after one edit only one object file is rebuilt](courses/diagrams/306c2ad6-54e8-5851-935e-3c5ffb59b65e/edit.svg)

Bonus: you can ship a library without its source, and people can work in parallel.

**Check:** you edit `kiosk.cpp`. What has to happen?

questions.question: You edit only the body of a function in `kiosk.cpp`. What has to happen before you run the program again?

lessons.title: Include Guards
lessons.readme:
# Include Guards

**The idea: an include guard stops one header from being pasted twice into the same file.**

`#include` literally pastes the header's text in. Paste a class twice and the compiler complains it's defined twice.

```cpp
#ifndef BOBACAFE_H      // "if not defined yet..."
#define BOBACAFE_H      // "...define it now"

class BobaCafe { /* ... */ };

#endif
```

The second paste sees `BOBACAFE_H` is defined and skips everything.

`#pragma once` does the same job. Almost every compiler has it, but it's **not standard** C++.

**Check:** what does `#pragma once` have that guards don't?

questions.question: What does an include guard prevent?
answers: Two `.cpp` files using the same header
Other files reading the private members
The header being compiled without any `.cpp`
One header pasted twice into the same file
questions.answer: One header pasted twice into the same file

questions.question: What is true of `#pragma once`?
answers: It makes the linker skip unchanged object files
It works like a guard but isn't standard C++
It must go at the bottom of the header file
It is the only standard form of include guard
questions.answer: It works like a guard but isn't standard C++

lessons.title: Is-A and Has-A
lessons.readme:
# Is-A and Has-A

**The idea: "is-a" means inheritance. "Has-a" means a member variable.**

![a food truck with an open service window and customers lining up](courses/diagrams/550505c3-2643-5438-b66b-7995a434a907/food-truck.jpg)
*Image: Kurtkaiser, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.*

The owner buys a food truck. A food truck **is a** cafe (it takes orders). A cafe **has a** tea brewer.

![an is-a arrow to the base class and has-a arrows to the members](courses/diagrams/550505c3-2643-5438-b66b-7995a434a907/both.svg)

```cpp
class MobileBobaCafe : public BobaCafe {   // is-a: inheritance
    float propane_remaining;               // has-a: composition
};
```

- **Base** (parent): the existing class, `BobaCafe`.
- **Derived** (child): the new one, `MobileBobaCafe`.

A `Menu` holding a `vector<Drink>` **has** drinks. A menu isn't a kind of drink, so no inheritance.

**Check:** a `Library` has a `Printer` member. Is-a or has-a?

lessons.title: What a Child Class Can Touch
lessons.readme:
# What a Child Class Can Touch

**The idea: a child class inherits everything, but can't touch the parent's private parts.**

Like inheriting a locked safe. It's yours, but you don't have the combination.

| In the base it's… | with `public` inheritance |
|---|---|
| public | stays public |
| private | inherited, but **inaccessible** |
| **protected** | usable by the child, hidden from `main` |

**Protected** is the middle option: private to the outside world, open to children.

> [!tip]
> Lab 8 has a protected `root`. When both classes are templates, the child must write `this->root`.

**Check:** which level hides a member from `main` but lets children use it?

questions.question: `Cart` publicly inherits from `Cafe`, which has `private: int cash;`. Inside a `Cart` method:
answers: `cash` is not part of a `Cart` at all
`cash` can be used like any own member

lessons.title: Extending the Cafe
lessons.readme:
# Extending the Cafe

**The idea: a child class adds new members, and builds its parent part first.**

![a mobile cafe object containing a whole base-class part](courses/diagrams/44b1fab1-a6ae-5fa3-b2bb-8205576019dc/parts.svg)

**Constructors aren't inherited.** Call the parent's in the init list:

```cpp
MobileBobaCafe() : BobaCafe(), propane_remaining(15.0f) {}
```

**Reuse the parent's method by naming it:**

```cpp
return BobaCafe::doOrder(customer_name);   // without BobaCafe:: it calls itself forever
```

> [!warning]
> This `doOrder` isn't `virtual`, so it only **hides** the parent's. A `BobaCafe&` to a truck still runs the plain cafe's version. Next lesson fixes that.

## Assignment

Finish the truck. Making one drink burns 1 unit of propane.

1. [ ] In the constructor's init list, start `propane_remaining` at 15.
2. [ ] `addPropane(amount)`: if `amount` is above 0, add it and return `true`. Otherwise return `false`.
3. [ ] `doOrder(customer_name)`: with 1 unit or less left, return an empty `Drink()`. Otherwise burn 1 unit and return what the base class's `doOrder` returns.

lessons.title: Virtual Functions
lessons.readme:
# Virtual Functions

**The idea: `virtual` makes the object's real type pick the method, not the pointer's type.**

A parent pointer can point at a child object. Which method runs?

**Without `virtual`:** the **pointer's** type decides, at compile time.

![without virtual the pointer type picks the function](courses/diagrams/be5110e3-6825-5df3-a950-93620046b7fd/plain.svg)

**With `virtual`:** the **object's** type decides, at run time (**dynamic dispatch**).

![with virtual the object type picks the function](courses/diagrams/be5110e3-6825-5df3-a950-93620046b7fd/virtual.svg)

Rules:
- Same for references.
- No override in the child? The **nearest parent** version runs.
- `virtual` must be on the **parent's** method.
- Deleting through a parent pointer? The parent's **destructor must be virtual**.

## Assignment

Make the brewers polymorphic.

1. [ ] Make `TeaBrewerImpl`'s destructor and its `addTea` virtual.
2. [ ] In `ColdBrewTeaBrewerImpl`, override `addTea` to set `tea_type` to `"Cold Brew"`.
3. [ ] Leave `DecafTeaBrewerImpl` empty and watch which version it gets.

lessons.title: Abstract Classes
lessons.readme:
# Abstract Classes

**The idea: `= 0` means "no body here. Every child must write its own."**

There's no such thing as a "brewer in general". Only specific kinds. So:

```cpp
virtual void addTea(Drink& d) = 0;   // pure virtual
```

![an abstract brewer with three derived classes](courses/diagrams/70ee0de4-5143-5b33-a703-dd31c084f20c/tree.svg)

A class with a pure virtual function is **abstract**. You **can't create** one. You **can** have pointers and references to it.

| | `virtual` | pure virtual `= 0` |
|---|---|---|
| has a body | yes | no |
| children | **may** override | **must** override |
| class is abstract | no | **yes** |

**Check:** what happens with `Pet pet;` if Pet is abstract?

questions.question: `virtual void f() {}` vs. `virtual void f() = 0;`. Which is true?
answers: Both can be overridden, and both make the class abstract
Only `= 0` uses dynamic dispatch through a base pointer
Both can be overridden; only `= 0` makes it abstract
Only `= 0` can be overridden by a derived class
questions.answer: Both can be overridden; only `= 0` makes it abstract

answers: Creates a derived object behind the scenes

lessons.title: Two Kinds of Polymorphism
lessons.readme:
# Two Kinds of Polymorphism

**The idea: polymorphism = one interface, many types. The right version is picked automatically.**

Like a "play" button. Same button for a song, a video or a podcast. Each plays its own way.

Two kinds:

- **Dynamic** (at run time): virtual functions.
- **Static** (at compile time): overloads like `price(int)` and `price(int, int)`, and templates.

Not polymorphism:
- Reusing a parent's members: that's **inheritance**.
- Hiding data behind an interface: that's **encapsulation**.

**Check:** which best describes polymorphism?

questions.question: Which best describes polymorphism?
answers: Several functions sharing one name with different parameter lists
One interface serving many types, picked at compile or run time
Data and functions bundled together behind a public interface
A derived class receiving the data and methods of its base class

lessons.title: Slicing
lessons.readme:
# Slicing

**The idea: copying a child into a plain parent variable cuts off the child part.**

Like photocopying only page 1 of a two-page form. Page 2 is gone.

![copying into a base object slices, a reference does not](courses/diagrams/b193fbb2-237e-583b-9fa2-4872fba4cf5f/slice.svg)

```cpp
Truck t;
Cafe copy = t;    // sliced: just a Cafe now
Cafe& ref = t;    // not sliced: still the truck
```

After slicing, even **virtual** calls run the parent version. The child part doesn't exist anymore.

**Check:** what do `copy.kind()` and `ref.kind()` print?

lessons.title: Tracing Constructors and Destructors
lessons.readme:
# Tracing Constructors and Destructors

**The idea: write output as objects are born and die. Locals die in reverse order.**

- **Constructor** prints when the object is made.
- **Destructor** prints at `delete`, or at the closing `}` for locals.
- Locals die **last-made first**.

```cpp
void f() {
    Cup a('a');              // +a
    Cup* b = new Cup('b');   // +b
    Cup c('c');              // +c
    delete b;                // -b
}                            // -c -a  (reverse order)
```

**Check:** trace `serve()` below.

lessons.title: Overloading Operators
lessons.readme:
# Overloading Operators

**The idea: operators are just functions with funny names.**

`a + b` can mean `a.operator+(b)`:

![a + b becomes a.operator+(b)](courses/diagrams/c7a28683-3593-5e8e-914a-bdeaf0d00eb0/call.svg)

```cpp
Vector2D operator+(const Vector2D& r) const {
    return Vector2D(x + r.x, y + r.y);
}
```

- A member operator has **one** parameter. The left side is already `*this`.
- It can read `r.x` even though it's private. Privacy is per class, not per object.
- Both `const`s: adding doesn't change either side.

Member is **one option, not a rule**. Next lesson shows free-function operators.

## Assignment

Add three member operators to `Vector2D`.

1. [ ] `operator+`, with one parameter.
2. [ ] `operator-`.
3. [ ] `operator==`: `true` only if **both** x and y match.

An error starting `no match for 'operator` names the one still missing.

lessons.title: Friend Functions
lessons.readme:
# Friend Functions

**The idea: a friend is an outside function the class lets see its private members.**

`cout << position` has the **stream** on the left. We can't add methods to the stream's class. So `<<` and `>>` **can't be members**. They must be outside functions, usually friends.

![members and friends reach private data, plain functions use getters](courses/diagrams/55c99635-64f4-5450-a86f-9631b17e60ba/who.svg)

`friend` goes **only** on the declaration inside the class:

```cpp
// inside the class
friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Vector2D& v);

// outside: no 'friend', no 'Vector2D::'
std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Vector2D& v) {
    return os << "(" << v.x << ", " << v.y << ")";   // return os so << chains
}
```

A non-member `+` takes **2** parameters, and allows `3 + v` (a member only allows `v + 3`).

## Assignment

1. [ ] Write `operator+` as a friend, so `3 + v` works.
2. [ ] Write a friend `operator<<` that prints `(x, y)`, like `(4, 6)`, and returns the stream.
3. [ ] Write a friend `operator>>` that reads x and then y, like `7 8`, and returns the stream.

It won't compile until all three exist.

lessons.title: Member or Free Operator?
lessons.readme:
# Member or Free Operator?

**The idea: most operators can be either. A few have no choice.**

| operator | member? | free function? |
|---|---|---|
| `+ - * / == <` and most | ok | ok |
| `<<`, `>>` with a stream | can't | **must** |
| `=`, `[]`, `()`, `->` | **must** | can't |

So "operators must be members" is **false**.

A free function can be:
- a **friend**: can read private members.
- a **plain** function: only uses public getters.

**Check:** a plain (non-friend) free function tries to read a private member. What happens?

questions.question: True or false: an overloaded `operator==` for a class has to be a member function of that class.
Which of these operators **must** be written as a member function?

answers: It compiles, but only `a - b` works and `b - a` does not
Compile error: `operator-` has to be a member function
It compiles: an operator may always read the class's private members
Compile error: `cents` is private and this function isn't a friend
questions.answer: Compile error: `cents` is private and this function isn't a friend

4. **Plain rule, said plainly.** No twist means true. Don't invent a trap.

lessons.title: Where Variables Live
lessons.readme:
# Where Variables Live

**The idea: your program sees memory as one huge array of bytes. A byte's address is its index.**

![two green DDR4 RAM sticks with black memory chips](courses/diagrams/4a1adf95-626f-5a68-803a-636473cfbcf3/ram.jpg)
*Image: Dsimic, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.*

Real hardware is messy (RAM, caches, SSDs). The operating system hides that behind **virtual memory**: one big, simple array.

Like house numbers on a long street. Every house has a number. That number is its **address**.

That big array is split into regions, highest address on top:

![memory regions from high address to low: args, stack, unused, heap, BSS, data, text](courses/diagrams/4a1adf95-626f-5a68-803a-636473cfbcf3/layout.svg)

**Check:** what is a memory address?

questions.question: In the lecture's picture of memory, what is an address?
answers: The index of a byte in one big array of bytes
The value currently stored inside the variable
The line number of the code
questions.answer: The index of a byte in one big array of bytes

questions.question: Which hides the messy real hardware behind one simple array of bytes?

lessons.title: Stack, Heap and the Rest
lessons.readme:
# Stack, Heap and the Rest

**The idea: locals live on the stack and vanish on return. Things made with `new` live on the heap until you `delete` them.**

| region | holds | lasts until |
|---|---|---|
| **stack** | locals, parameters | the function returns |
| **heap** | anything from `new` | you `delete` it |
| **BSS** | globals/statics with no start value | program ends |
| **data** | globals/statics with a start value | program ends |
| **text** | your compiled code | program ends |

The stack grows **down** (toward lower addresses). The heap grows **up**. They grow toward each other.

Think of the stack as a pile of plates: each call adds a plate, each return takes it off.

**Check:** where does a global `int visits = 42;` live?

questions.question: A global `int visits = 42;` (it has a starting value) lives in:
As more functions get called, the stack grows toward:

lessons.title: Stack or Heap?
lessons.readme:
# Stack or Heap?

**The idea: a variable declared in a function is on the stack. The thing `new` makes is on the heap.**

```cpp
int main() {
    Room* r = new Room();   // r itself: stack.  the Room it points to: heap
    Room spare = *r;        // spare: stack (a copy)
    delete r;               // frees the heap Room. r is still on the stack
}
```

![r on the stack points to a Room on the heap; spare is a separate Room on the stack](courses/diagrams/f30f5024-bd36-5324-a3d9-a4debd984ba3/pic.svg)

`spare` is a **new** Room on the stack, copied from the heap one. Not shared.

**Why use the heap?** Lifetime. A heap object survives after the function returns, so a function can make it and hand it back.

**Check:** where does `spot` live?

questions.question: Which of these is still alive after the function that created it returns?
answers: The pointer that held new's result

lessons.title: Pointers: An Address Plus a Type
lessons.readme:
# Pointers: An Address Plus a Type

**The idea: a pointer is a variable that holds an address, plus the type of what's there.**

Like a note that says "the keys are in drawer 3". The note isn't the keys. It tells you where they are.

```cpp
int beds = 4;
int* pb = &beds;     // pb holds the address of beds
```

![pb holds the address of beds](courses/diagrams/a25600e8-8b36-5576-a4d5-397cd1fe06fb/pic.svg)

`pb` is its own variable, with its own address. The value inside it is `beds`'s address. The type `int*` says "an int lives there".

**Check:** what does `pb` itself store?

questions.question: What does the pointer variable `pb` itself store?
answers: A copy of the value in `beds`

questions.question: In one phrase, what is a pointer?
answers: A second name bound to an existing variable
An address paired with the type stored there
A variable that can only exist on the stack
An object that releases its own memory
questions.answer: An address paired with the type stored there

lessons.title: Address-Of and Dereference
lessons.readme:
# Address-Of and Dereference

**The idea: `&x` gets x's address. `*p` follows the pointer to the thing it points at.**

| operator | name | gives you |
|---|---|---|
| `&beds` | address-of | where beds lives |
| `*pb` | dereference | the thing pb points at |

Writing through `*pb` changes the real variable:

```cpp
*pb = 6;        // beds is now 6
```

Things a pointer is **not**:
- Not another name for a variable (that's a reference).
- Not tied to the stack.
- Not a way to free memory.

**Check:** what does the code below print?

questions.question: `int x = 3; int* p = &x;` Which expression gives the value 3?

lessons.title: Pointers to Pointers
lessons.readme:
# Pointers to Pointers

**The idea: each `*` follows one arrow. Count the stars.**

A pointer is a variable, so it has an address too. You can point at it.

```cpp
int floor = 3;
int* pf = &floor;      // 1 arrow to floor
int** ppf = &pf;       // 2 arrows to floor
int*** pppf = &ppf;    // 3 arrows to floor
```

![pppf points to ppf, which points to pf, which points to floor](courses/diagrams/e9d6226d-2166-5a53-bbe8-86b71b83e8c0/pic.svg)

**Shortcut:** stars in the type minus stars you apply = what's left. `pppf` is `int***`. Apply 2 stars → `int*`, an address.

> [!warning]
> `&(&floor)` is illegal. `&floor` is a temporary value with no address of its own.

**Check:** what is `**pppf`?

questions.question: Is `int** ppf = &(&floor);` legal C++?
answers: No, `&floor` is a temporary with no address
Yes, but only if `floor` is const
Yes, it gives the same address as `&pf` would
No, because `int**` cannot hold an address
questions.answer: No, `&floor` is a temporary with no address

lessons.title: Swap Through Pointers
lessons.readme:
# Swap Through Pointers

**The idea: pass addresses, and a function can change the caller's variables.**

```cpp
int x = 214, y = 108;
swapPtr(&x, &y);     // now x is 108, y is 214
```

Inside, save one **value** in a temp, then copy:

![swap steps 1 and 2](courses/diagrams/9cad54e5-597c-5c26-83f6-6b68a106922b/a.svg)

![swap step 3 and the result](courses/diagrams/9cad54e5-597c-5c26-83f6-6b68a106922b/b.svg)

1. `int tmp = *a;` saves 214.
2. `*a = *b;` copies 108 into x.
3. `*b = tmp;` puts 214 into y.

Every line that does work has a `*` on the left.

> [!warning]
> `int* t = a; a = b; b = t;` only swaps the local pointers. The caller sees nothing.

## Assignment

This starts `rooms.h`, a file of room helpers we'll keep adding to.

1. [ ] Complete `swapPtr(a, b)` so it swaps the two ints that `a` and `b` point at.

It must also work when both point at the same int, and on array elements like `swapPtr(&rooms[0], &rooms[1])`.

lessons.readme:
# Swap Traps

**The idea: save the value (`int tmp = *a`), never the address (`int* tmp = a`).**

**Trap 1: won't compile.**
```cpp
int* tmp = *a;      // *a is an int, tmp wants an address
```

**Trap 2: compiles, wrong answer.**
```cpp
int* tmp = a;       // tmp points at the SAME int as a
*a = *b;            // that int is overwritten...
*b = *tmp;          // ...so this reads the new value
```

With x = 1, y = 2 you get `2 2`. The old value is gone.

Like writing a phone number on your hand by pointing at the contact card, then erasing the card.

> [!tip]
> Draw a box per variable and an arrow per pointer. Change one box per line.

**Check:** trace `swapBad` below.

questions.question: What happens with `int* tmp = *a;` inside a swap function where `a` is an `int*`?

lessons.title: References
lessons.readme:
# References

**The idea: a reference is just another name for a variable that already exists.**

Like a nickname. "Bob" and "Robert" are the same person.

```cpp
int beds = 2;
int& r = beds;     // r is another name for beds
r = 5;             // beds is 5
beds++;            // r sees 6
```

![one int with two names](courses/diagrams/36167b4e-c3e9-5769-a4c3-ca4d634e16d0/pic.svg)

No copy. No `*` needed. Changing one changes "both", because there's only one.

> [!note]
> `&` means different things by spot: `&i` = address-of, `int& r` = reference, `a && b` = logical AND.

**Check:** what prints below?

lessons.title: References vs Pointers
lessons.readme:
# References vs Pointers

**The idea: references give up flexibility in exchange for safety.**

| | pointer | reference |
|---|---|---|
| leave it unset at first | yes | **no**: `int& r;` won't compile |
| can be null | yes | no |
| point somewhere else later | yes | no, stuck forever |
| needs `*` to use | yes | no |
| arithmetic, `int**` levels | yes | no |

Fewer abilities, but no null checks and cleaner code. The lecture's advice: **prefer references when you can.**

**Check:** what can a pointer do that a reference can't?

questions.question: Does `int& r;` (with nothing after it) compile?
answers: Yes, it starts out as null
Yes, it refers to a hidden temporary 0
No, a reference must be initialized
questions.answer: No, a reference must be initialized

questions.question: Which of these can a pointer do that a reference cannot?
answers: Modify the value of the original object
Point at a different object later
questions.answer: Point at a different object later

lessons.title: Pass by Value

questions.question: A function takes `int count` and sets `count = 0;`. What happens to the caller's variable?
answers: It becomes 0 as soon as it returns

lessons.title: Pass by Reference
lessons.readme:
# Pass by Reference

**The idea: add `&` to the parameter, and the function works on the caller's real variable.**

```cpp
void square(int& i) { i = i * i; }
int main() { int i = 5; square(i); cout << i; }   // 25
```

![square refers to main's i](courses/diagrams/ba9e6a38-b7fe-5e41-b102-eb6ea181ca44/pic.svg)

No copy is made. The change sticks.

The lecture calls this **bad style** for `square`: reading `square(i)`, nobody would guess `i` changes. Only do it when changing the variable is clearly the job (like swap).

**Check:** trace `grow` below.

lessons.title: Const References
lessons.readme:
# Const References

**The idea: `const T&` = no copy, and no changes allowed. Best for big objects you only read.**

Like letting a friend look at your phone, but not touch it.

```cpp
void square(const int& i) {
    i = i * i;          // compile error: read-only
}
int square(const int& i) {
    return i * i;       // fine: just reads
}
```

| parameter | copies? | can change caller? |
|---|---|---|
| `int i` | yes | no |
| `int& i` | no | yes |
| `const int& i` | no | no |
| `int* p` | copies the address | yes, through `*p` |

**Check:** what happens when `square(const int& i)` assigns to `i`?

answers: It runs but the result is undefined

lessons.title: Returning a Reference
lessons.readme:
# Returning a Reference

**The idea: never return a reference or pointer to a local variable. It dies when the function returns.**

Like giving someone directions to a tent you're about to pack up.

```cpp
const int& square(const int& i) {
    int res = i * i;
    return res;         // BUG: res dies right here
}
```

![main holds a reference into square's frame, which no longer exists](courses/diagrams/e5abdbc3-8af2-5906-b791-6d699f8721cd/pic.svg)

That's a **dangling reference**. It might print the right number once, then break later.

Safe: returning a reference to the **caller's** variable, or returning **by value**.

Two wrong explanations to rule out:
- It **does** compile (at most a warning).
- It's **not** a leak. Nothing was made with `new`.

**Check:** which function dangles?

questions.question: Which function returns a dangling reference?
answers: `const int& f(int& i) { int r = i*i; i = r; return i; }`
`int f(const int& i) { int r = i*i; return r; }`
`const int& f(const int& i) { int r = i*i; return r; }`
questions.answer: `const int& f(const int& i) { int r = i*i; return r; }`

answers: It leaks memory, because `out` is never deleted
It is safe, because `x` is passed in by reference
Unsafe: it returns a reference to a destroyed local
It fails to compile, because `out` is changed with `-=`
questions.answer: Unsafe: it returns a reference to a destroyed local

answers: Undefined: it returns a dangling reference

lessons.title: const and Pointers
lessons.readme:
# const and Pointers

**The idea: find the `*`. `const` on its left locks the object. `const` on its right locks the pointer.**

Read declarations **right to left**:

```cpp
const River* p;          // pointer to a const River
River* const p = &x;     // const pointer to a River
const River* const p = &x;   // both locked
```

| declaration | change the River? | point elsewhere? |
|---|---|---|
| `const River* p` | no | yes |
| `River* const p` | yes | no |
| `const River* const p` | no | no |

![three pointer declarations: const on the left of the star locks the River, const on the right locks the pointer](courses/diagrams/9eb4b762-1d30-58b9-897f-611623c9dedb/pic.svg)

**Check:** what does `River* const p` declare?

questions.question: `River* const p = &nile;` declares:
answers: A pointer to a const River
A const pointer to a River
A const copy of a River
A const reference to a River
questions.answer: A const pointer to a River

lessons.title: new and delete
lessons.readme:
# new and delete

**The idea: `new` makes an object on the heap and gives you its address. `delete` destroys it.**

```cpp
Room* r = new Room();    // make one Room, run its constructor
delete r;                // run its destructor, free the memory
```

**Every `new` needs exactly one `delete`.** C++ has no garbage collector.

Only delete pointers that came from `new`:

```cpp
int* p = new int();   // from new: delete it once
int* q = p;           // a copy: same object, don't delete twice
int i;
int* s = &i;          // address of a local: NEVER delete
```

![before and after delete: r still holds the old address](courses/diagrams/f87429ba-2873-587d-a468-c394aa7d47d7/pic.svg)

> [!warning]
> `delete r;` doesn't change `r`. It still holds the old address.

**Check:** what's wrong with deleting `&count`?

questions.question: What does `new Room()` return?
answers: The address of the new Room
A copy of the new Room
The size of a Room in bytes
A reference to the new Room
questions.answer: The address of the new Room

lessons.title: new[] and delete[]
lessons.readme:
# new[] and delete[]

**The idea: `new[]` pairs with `delete[]`. Mixing them up is undefined behavior.**

```cpp
Room* floor = new Room[4];   // 4 Rooms, constructor runs 4 times
delete[] floor;              // destructor runs 4 times
```

![floor on the stack points at element 0 of four Rooms on the heap](courses/diagrams/d5952d36-c464-57a5-9571-bc856fd792f0/pic.svg)

`floor` holds the address of element `[0]`.

| allocate | free | runs |
|---|---|---|
| `new T()` | `delete p` | 1 |
| `new T[n]` | `delete[] p` | n |

Plain `delete` on an array treats it as one object. Bad.

**Check:** what's wrong with `delete list;` after `new Song[6]`?

answers: `list` must be set to nullptr first
Objects cannot be allocated as arrays

questions.question: After `delete[] scores;`, what does `scores` hold?
answers: The value of its first element

questions.question: How many times does the constructor run for `new Room[5]`?

lessons.title: Memory Leaks
lessons.readme:
# Memory Leaks

**The idea: a leak is heap memory that nothing points to anymore. Nobody can ever free it.**

Like a balloon you let go of. It's still out there, but you can't grab it.

You lose the last pointer by **reassigning** it, **returning** without deleting, or **overwriting** it.

```cpp
int* p = new int[8];
int* q = new int[3];
int* r = p;       // second arrow to the 8-block (not a new block)
q = p;            // the 3-block just lost its only arrow: LEAK
delete[] r;       // frees the 8-block, once
```

![after q = p, nothing points at the 3-int block](courses/diagrams/42685868-f5b0-5aa5-a673-674351eca401/pic.svg)

Copying a pointer copies the **arrow**, not the block.

**Check:** trace the second example. What leaks?

lessons.title: Dangling Pointers
lessons.readme:
# Dangling Pointers

**The idea: a dangling pointer points at memory that's already been freed.**

A leak = memory nobody points at. Dangling = a pointer to memory that's gone.

```cpp
delete[] floor;
floor[0].print();     // BUG: floor still holds the old address
```

Ways to get one:
- Use a pointer after `delete`.
- **Delete twice**: `int* q = p; delete p; delete q;`
- Keep `&local` after the local is gone.

**Habit:** set it to `nullptr` right after deleting.

```cpp
delete[] floor;
floor = nullptr;      // deleting nullptr again is harmless
```

**Check:** what's the problem with `delete p; delete q;` when `q = p`?

answers: `q` is a separate copy of the int
Nothing, each pointer is deleted once
The same block is deleted twice
questions.answer: The same block is deleted twice

lessons.title: C-Style Arrays
lessons.readme:
# C-Style Arrays

**The idea: a C-style array is a fixed row of boxes, side by side, numbered from 0. No safety checks.**

```cpp
int freeBeds[15];     // freeBeds[0] to freeBeds[14]
```

- **Fixed length**, set when it's made.
- **Contiguous**: boxes sit right next to each other.
- **Starts at 0.**
- **No bounds check**: `freeBeds[15] = 1;` compiles and writes past the end. Undefined behavior.
- **Starts with garbage** if it's a local and you don't fill it.

It skips safety to be fast.

**Check:** what happens with `beds[4] = 9;` on a 4-element array?

answers: A compile error: index out of range

lessons.title: Searching an Array
lessons.readme:
# Searching an Array

**The idea: check each element. Return true the moment you find it. Return false only after checking them all.**

This is **linear search**. Quizzes ask you to write it by hand:

```cpp
bool hasRoom(const int rooms[], int len, int room) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        if (rooms[i] == room) return true;   // found: stop now
    }
    return false;                            // checked all: not there
}
```

`return true` goes **inside** the loop. `return false` goes **after** it.

> [!warning]
> Points get taken off for:
> - `return false` in an `else` inside the loop (gives up after one element).
> - No `return false` at all.
> - Wrong bounds (`i < len - 1` or `i <= len`).
> - Asking a C array for `.size()`. Use `len`.

Worst case checks all n elements: O(n).

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `hasRoom(rooms, len, room)`: return `true` if `room` is among the first `len` elements of `rooms`, and `false` otherwise.

lessons.readme:
# Array Operations Big O

**The idea: arrays are instant to read by index, but slow to insert into the middle.**

A data structure = what it can do **and** how fast.

| operation | Big O | why |
|---|---|---|
| read or change `arr[i]` | O(1) | address = start + i × size |
| add to the end | O(1) | if there's room |
| add/remove at start or middle | O(n) | shift everything after it |
| find a value | O(n) | check each one |

Like a row of numbered lockers. Opening locker 37 is instant. Squeezing a new locker in the middle means moving every locker after it.

`insertAt` at index 0 shifts n − 1 elements: O(n) worst case.

**Check:** why is `arr[i]` O(1)?

Why is reading `arr[i]` O(1) for any i?
answers: It checks each element until it gets to i
Its address is computed directly from i
questions.answer: Its address is computed directly from i

lessons.title: Shallow Copies
lessons.readme:
# Shallow Copies

**The idea: the default copy copies the pointer, not what it points to. Two objects end up sharing one array.**

Like copying a house key instead of building a second house. Both keys open the same door.

```cpp
myArray<int> a(50);
myArray<int> b = a;     // default copy
b[0] = 2;               // changes a[0] too!
```

![a and b both point at the same heap array](courses/diagrams/2d72f1ca-7fe7-566c-905c-d75399421d65/pic.svg)

That's a **shallow copy**. Worse: both destructors `delete[]` the same array (a double delete).

We want a **deep copy**: the new object gets its own array, with each element copied in.

**Check:** what does `a[1]` print below?

questions.question: For a pointer member like `T* array`, the default copy constructor copies:
answers: Nothing, it sets it to nullptr

lessons.title: The Copy Constructor
lessons.readme:
# The Copy Constructor

**The idea: a copy constructor gives the new object its own array, then copies every element.**

```cpp
IntArray(const IntArray& other) : data(new int[other.n]), n(other.n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) data[i] = other.data[i];
}
```

![a and b each point at their own heap array](courses/diagrams/cef9f2c4-b7a0-5add-b7ed-40864953a0cf/pic.svg)

- Take the source **by const reference**. By value would need a copy to make a copy, forever.
- Now each object has its own array. Each destructor deletes its own.

> [!warning]
> `data` is declared before `n`, so it's set first. Use `other.n`, not `n`, in `data`'s initializer.

## Assignment

The starter's copy constructor is the shallow default, written out.

1. [ ] Make it a deep copy: allocate a new array of `other.n` ints and copy every element into it.

Submit also checks pass-by-value copies, `IntArray c(b)`, and copying an empty `IntArray(0)`.

lessons.readme:
# When the Copy Constructor Runs

**The idea: the copy constructor runs when a new object is being created from another. Not when one already exists.**

Runs:
```cpp
IntArray b = a;    // b is being created (even with =)
IntArray c(a);     // same thing
show(a);           // show(IntArray x): passed by value
```

Doesn't run:
```cpp
peek(a);           // peek(const IntArray& x): reference, no copy
b = a;             // b already exists: this is operator=
```

The `=` sign doesn't decide it. Ask: **is the left side being born on this line?**

**Check:** count the copy constructor calls below.

lessons.title: The Assignment Operator
lessons.readme:
# The Assignment Operator

**The idea: `b = a` (when b exists) needs four steps: guard, delete, copy, return.**

From the Lab 2 solution:

```cpp
IntArray& operator=(const IntArray& other) {
    if (this == &other) return *this;   // 1. a = a? do nothing
    delete[] data;                      // 2. free the old array
    n = other.n;                        // 3. new array, deep copy
    data = new int[n];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) data[i] = other.data[i];
    return *this;                       // 4. so a = b = c works
}
```

![operator= frees the old array, then allocates and copies](courses/diagrams/d80ef973-6ba9-5d53-b7df-2c9f3ff6b8a2/pic.svg)

1. **Guard:** `a = a` would delete the data, then copy from it.
2. **Delete:** or the old array leaks.
3. **Reallocate:** sizes may differ.
4. **Return `*this`:** `a = (b = c)` needs `b` back.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Add `operator=` to `IntArray` with all four steps. It must return `IntArray&`.

Tests check self-assignment, smaller and bigger sources, chaining, returning the object itself, and no leaks.

lessons.title: The Rule of Three
lessons.readme:
# The Rule of Three

**The idea: if a class needs a destructor, a copy constructor, or `operator=`, it needs all three.**

A class that **owns heap memory** needs:

1. a **destructor**: to free it,
2. a **copy constructor**: so a new copy gets its own,
3. an **assignment operator**: free the old, deep copy the new.

That's the **rule of three**. The trigger is usually a raw pointer the class owns.

| you write `b = a;` and... | what runs |
|---|---|
| b is being created | copy constructor |
| b already exists | `operator=` |
| an object dies | destructor |

**Check:** a class has a destructor that frees an array. What else does it need?

answers: To avoid calling the copy constructor

# Writing a Class Template

**The idea: outside the class, every member needs the `template` line and `<T>` after the class name.**

```cpp
template <typename T>                    // 1. repeat on EVERY member
T& myArray<T>::operator[](int idx) {     // 2. myArray<T>::, with <T>
    if (idx < 0 || idx >= allocated_size) {
        abort();                         // bad index: stop the program
    }
    return array[idx];
}
```

This `operator[]` adds the bounds check C arrays don't have.

> [!warning]
> Template code goes **entirely in the header**. The compiler needs the full code to make `myArray<int>`.

## Assignment

The constructor and destructor in `myarray.h` are written outside the class as examples. Until you add the two below, the build says "undefined reference".

1. [ ] Below them, define `size()`, outside the class. It returns `allocated_size`.
2. [ ] Define `operator[]`, outside the class. It returns a reference to element `idx`, and calls `abort()` if `idx < 0` or `idx >= allocated_size`.

Tests use `myArray<int>` and `myArray<std::string>`. Submit also checks that `-1` and `size()` abort.

# Template Rules

**The idea: three rules cover almost every template question.**

1. **Outside the class:** repeat `template <typename T>` and write `myArray<T>::`.
2. **Header only:** the full code lives in the `.h`.
3. **Name the type when you use it:** `myArray<int> a(50);`.

| | bad index |
|---|---|

| `std::vector` `[]` | no check: undefined behavior |

# STL Containers

**The idea: the STL is a ready-made toolbox of data structures that comes with C++.**

| `std::` | what it is |
|---|---|
| `array` | fixed-size array |
| `vector` | array that grows |
| `list` | doubly linked list |
| `deque` | fast at both ends |
| `stack`, `queue` | built on `deque` |
| `priority_queue` | max-heap |
| `unordered_map` | hash table |
| `map` | sorted tree |

None of these are **fundamental types**. Those are built into the language: `int`, `char`, `double`, `bool`.

lessons.title: Walking a List with Iterators
lessons.readme:
# Walking a List with Iterators

**The idea: an iterator is like a bookmark that knows how to move to the next element.**

A `std::list` has no `[i]`. So you walk it with an iterator:

```cpp
for (std::list<int>::iterator it = beds.begin(); it != beds.end(); ++it)
    cout << *it;
```

- `begin()`: the first element.
- `end()`: **one past the last**. A stop sign. Never use `*` on it.
- `*it` reads the element. `++it` moves forward.

![a list of three with begin on the first node, an iterator on the second, and end one past the last](courses/diagrams/681c676f-8a52-520c-8f26-e23264316043/pic.svg)

Shorter version, the **range-based for**:

```cpp
for (auto& b : beds) b += 1;   // & : changes the real element
for (auto b : beds) b += 1;    // BUG: changes a copy
```

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `totalFree(beds)`: return the sum of all the elements. Use an explicit iterator loop with `begin()` and `end()`.
2. [ ] Complete `addBeds(beds, k)`: add `k` to every element of the list, using a range-based for loop.

An empty list has a total of 0.

# Pointer Tracing Review

**The idea: boxes for variables, arrows for pointers, one line at a time.**

- `*p = ...` changes the **box** the arrow points at.
- `p = ...` moves the **arrow**.
- A reference is a second **name** on a box.
- `p + 2` moves 2 **elements**, not 2 bytes.

| code | means |
|---|---|

| `*p = 5;` | x becomes 5 |
| `int& r = x;` | r is another name for x |
| `r = y;` | x gets y's **value** |
| `int** pp = &p;` | `**pp` is x |

# Why Analyze Algorithms?

**The idea: count the steps an algorithm takes, and see how the count grows as the input grows.**

The lecture's insertion sort took **22 seconds** on 75,000 ints. `std::sort` took a tiny fraction of that.

```cpp
for (auto i = lst.begin(); i != lst.end(); ++i)
    for (auto j = lst.begin(); j != i; ++j)
        if (*i < *j) { T temp = *i; *i = *j; *j = temp; }
```

Count: the inner loop runs 0, then 1, then 2, … up to n − 1 times. Total ≈ **n²/2**. We say it's **"order n squared."**

Double the list → about **4 times** the work.

Why count instead of timing it? Counting works for every input, every computer, every language.

**Check:** the list triples. How much more work?

It gives the exact running time in seconds
The result holds for any input, computer and language
questions.answer: The result holds for any input, computer and language

# Constants and Lower Terms

**The idea: for big n, only the biggest term matters, and constant multipliers don't change the growth rate.**

How much of n² + 4n + 20 is just the n²?

| n | n²'s share |
|---|---|
| 10 | 63% |
| 100 | 96% |
| 1000 | 99.6% |

So n² + 4n + 20 is just **quadratic**. 3n + 25 is just **linear**.

**But constants matter for small n.** Insertion sort (≈ n²/4) beats merge sort (≈ 2n log n) on small lists. On a million items, insertion sort takes 70 hours, merge sort 40 seconds.

# Big-Oh: The Definition

**The idea: f(n) is O(g(n)) means a scaled-up g(n) is a ceiling for f(n), once n is big enough.**

Like saying "my commute is at most twice the distance in minutes, once I'm past the parking lot".

The definition, word for word (put it on your note sheet):

**f(n) is O(g(n)) if there are positive constants c and n₀ such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀.**

![3n plus 25 and 4n crossing at n equals 25](courses/diagrams/d5b85953-d692-5a8f-9703-ac3fa45dcded/ceiling.svg)

Before n₀, f can be above the ceiling. That's allowed.

**Check:** what does the definition promise?

From some n₀ on, c·g(n) is a ceiling on f(n)
f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for every n, starting at n = 1
c·g(n) bounds f(n) from above and below

# Disproving Big-Oh

**The idea: to show f is NOT O(g), suppose some c works, then find an n that breaks it.**

**Claim: 3n + 25 is not O(1).** (So c·g(n) is just c.)

1. **Suppose it is:** 3n + 25 ≤ c for all n ≥ n₀.
2. **Solve for n:** n ≤ (c − 25)/3.
3. **Break it:** pick n bigger than both n₀ and (c − 25)/3. The inequality fails.
4. **Contradiction.** No c works.

Like claiming "this bucket holds any amount of water". Just pour in more than it holds.

Same pattern: n² is not O(n), because n² ≤ c·n means n ≤ c, and any n > c breaks it.

**Check:** which n breaks 2n + 7 ≤ c?

Any n that is smaller than (c − 7)/2
Only n = n₀, where the bound starts
Any n bigger than both n₀ and (c − 7)/2

lessons.title: Tight and Loose Bounds
lessons.readme:
# Tight and Loose Bounds

**The idea: Big-Oh is only a ceiling, so a too-high ceiling is still true. Just not useful.**

"4n² is O(n³)" is **true**. It's **loose**. "4n² is O(n²)" is **tight**.

Like saying "the movie is under 10 hours". True, but not helpful.

Rules for stating a bound:
1. Drop lower terms.
2. Drop constants.
3. Use the **smallest** class that works.
4. Write it the **simplest** way: O(n), not O(3n).

> [!warning]
> On "which is false?", a loose bound is still **true**. Look for one where f grows **faster** than g.

**Check:** which statement is false?

lessons.title: The Analysis Process
lessons.readme:
# The Analysis Process

**The idea: five steps turn any code into a Big-Oh.**

1. **Inputs:** list every size that can vary.
2. **Control flow:** how many times does each loop run?
3. **Cost per pass:** simple operations are O(1). A function call costs **its** Big-Oh.
4. **Combine:** sequential adds, nested uses the counts.
5. **Simplify** to the biggest term.

**Worked example:**

```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < i; j++)
        checkClash(i, j);
```

(1) n. (2) inner runs i times. (3) O(1). (4) 0 + 1 + … + (n − 1) = n(n − 1)/2. (5) **O(n²)**.

![six by six grid with the cells below the diagonal highlighted](courses/diagrams/db6e65b2-0976-5d0d-a0fc-d455153dc271/pairs.svg)

**Check:** with n = 40, how many calls?

lessons.title: Checking Every Pair
lessons.readme:
# Checking Every Pair

**The idea: `j < i` visits every pair exactly once.**

Like a handshake round: each person shakes hands with everyone **before** them in line. No one shakes their own hand. No pair shakes twice.

| inner loop | pairs visited |
|---|---|
| `j < i` | each pair once |
| `j < n` | each pair **twice**, plus self-pairs |

That's n(n − 1)/2 checks: O(n²).

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `countClashes(start)`. `start[i]` is the start hour of section i. Return how many **pairs** of sections share a start hour.
2. [ ] Use nested loops with `j < i`, so every pair is checked exactly once.

Example: `{9, 10, 9, 13, 10, 9}` has three 9s (3 pairs) and two 10s (1 pair), so the answer is 4.

lessons.title: Nested Loops
lessons.readme:
# Nested Loops

**The idea: if the inner loop runs the same number of times every pass, multiply.**

```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++)
        work();        // n · n = n² times
```

A loop with a **fixed** count is just a constant: `j < 50` → n · 50 → **O(n)**.

**Exact counts:** with `j < n/2`, each row has n/2 cells:

![six by six grid with the first three columns highlighted in every row](courses/diagrams/fdc166f5-578f-5dcb-b171-d6b0cbfcbd8a/half.svg)

That's **n²/2** exactly. Still O(n²). A step of `j += 2` gives the same n/2 per row.

> [!warning]
> Only multiply when the inner count **doesn't** depend on i. Otherwise, add them up (next lesson).

**Check:** exactly how many times does `work()` run with `j < n / 2`?

lessons.title: Dependent Inner Loops
lessons.readme:
# Dependent Inner Loops

**The idea: when the inner count depends on i, make a table and add up the column.**

```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < i * i; j++)
        work();
```

| i | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | … |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| inner runs | 0 | 1 | 4 | 9 | 16 | … |

![bars of length 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25](courses/diagrams/8d53207e-538d-5d88-a308-be067ad8efff/squares.svg)

0² + 1² + … + (n − 1)² ≈ **n³/3**. That's **O(n³)**, from only two loops.

Two sums for your note sheet:
- 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2
- 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2ᵏ = 2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1

**Check:** what's the Big-Oh of the loop above?

lessons.title: Counting Halvings
lessons.readme:
# Counting Halvings

**The idea: halving n over and over reaches 1 after log₂ n steps.**

Like folding a paper strip in half until it's one square wide.

![n goes 16, 8, 4, 2, 1](courses/diagrams/547918e2-e61f-5fab-9194-98e769216485/halvings.svg)

16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1: four halvings. log₂ 16 = 4.

Why: after k halvings, n/2ᵏ is left. Set that to 1: 2ᵏ = n, so **k = log₂ n**.

Write this on the exam: "each pass halves n; after k passes n/2ᵏ = 1, so k = log₂ n passes of O(1) work: **O(log n)**."

## Assignment

Lab 3 had this exact helper.

1. [ ] Complete `countHalvings(n)`: while `n > 1`, halve n with integer division and count the step. Return the count.

`countHalvings(16)` is 4, `countHalvings(17)` is 4 (17 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1), `countHalvings(1)` is 0.

lessons.title: Logarithmic Loops
lessons.readme:
# Logarithmic Loops

**The idea: a loop whose counter is multiplied or divided each pass runs about log n times.**

Binary search halves what's left each pass:

![binary search for 23 in 16 sorted values: each pass looks at the middle and throws away half](courses/diagrams/026a233e-6cf2-59f9-9f9f-cff3b54024cf/trace.svg)

n, n/2, n/4, … → log₂ n passes of O(1) work: **O(log n)**.

Same for `i *= 2`, `i /= 2`, `i *= 3`. The base doesn't matter.

**Combine with other loops by multiplying.** Lab 3's `func1`:

```cpp
int bound = countHalvings(n);       // runs once: log n
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < bound; j++)
        for (int k = 0; k < bound; k++)
            num_iterations++;
```

n · log n · log n = **O(n log² n)**.

**Check:** about how many passes on 1,000,000 items?

questions.question: What is the Big-Oh of `func1` above?
Binary search on 1,000,000 sorted IDs runs at most about how many passes?

lessons.title: The Doubling-Loop Trap
lessons.readme:
# The Doubling-Loop Trap

**The idea: when i doubles and the inner loop runs i times, the total is about 2n, so O(n). Not O(n log n).**

This was on the midterm:

```cpp
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i *= 2)
    for (int j = 0; j < i; j++)
        work();
```

The inner loop runs 1, 2, 4, 8, … times. Add them:

![bars of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 adding to 31](courses/diagrams/93e2e892-483a-560b-b2a4-abe6d04a9bc8/trap.svg)

1 + 2 + 4 + … + n = **2n − 1**. **O(n)**.

With `j < n` instead, every row is full:

![five bars of 16 adding to 80](courses/diagrams/93e2e892-483a-560b-b2a4-abe6d04a9bc8/full.svg)

That one really is **O(n log n)**.

**Check:** with n = 64, exactly how many runs?

lessons.title: More Than One Input
lessons.readme:
# More Than One Input

**The idea: keep every input size as its own letter. Don't squash them into one n.**

**One after the other: add.**
```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += a[i];   // n students
for (int j = 0; j < m; j++) sum += b[j];   // m sections
```
→ **O(n + m)**. Nobody said m is close to n.

**A grid:** rows × cols → **O(rows · cols)**.

**Calls inside loops multiply.** Sort each of n vectors of size k:
```cpp
for (auto& inner : v) std::sort(inner.begin(), inner.end());
```
→ n × O(k log k) = **O(n · k log k)**.

**Check:** two loops, one after the other, over n and m. Big-Oh?

# Counting Unique Values

**The idea: use a checklist with one box per possible value. Tick each value the first time you see it.**

lessons.title: Unique Values Big O
lessons.readme:
# Unique Values Big O

**The idea: the biggest value k is a second input. `countUnique` is O(n + k).**

**Step 1, inputs:** n = how many values. **k = the max value.**

| part | cost |
|---|---|
| find the max | O(n) |
| make `seen` with k + 1 slots | O(k) |
| loop over v | O(n) |

Total: **O(n + k) time, O(k) space.**

Why not just O(n)? Five values with max 9000: n = 5, but making `seen` costs 9000.

The trade: spend O(k) memory so each "seen it?" check is O(1). Comparing every pair would use no memory but take O(n²).

**Check:** what is the extra space?

lessons.title: Counting Sort
lessons.readme:
# Counting Sort

**The idea: don't compare values. Count how many of each, then write them back in order.**

Like sorting exam papers by score: make a pile for each score, drop each paper in its pile, then stack the piles.

Lab 3's `func3`:

1. Find `minVal` and `maxVal`. You need `maxVal - minVal + 1` slots.
2. For each value, add 1 to `count[v[i] - minVal]`. (Subtracting `minVal` puts the smallest at slot 0, so negatives work.)
3. Walk the slots in order and write each value back `count[val]` times.

v = {2, −1, 3, 0, 2, −1, 2}, min = −1, max = 3:

![v and its count array](courses/diagrams/d9903376-e585-5a55-9e21-1986074e95d1/count.svg)

![count array written back into v in order](courses/diagrams/d9903376-e585-5a55-9e21-1986074e95d1/write.svg)

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `getMinVal(v)`: return the smallest value. You can assume v isn't empty.
2. [ ] Complete `countingSort(v)` so it sorts v ascending, in place, using the three steps. If v is empty, do nothing.

Values may be negative. `getMaxVal` is already done.

lessons.title: Counting Sort Big O
lessons.readme:
# Counting Sort Big O

**The idea: when the inner loop counts add up to n, add instead of multiply.**

The write-back loops:

```cpp
for (int val = 0; val < range; val++)
    for (int c = 0; c < count[val]; c++)
        v[index++] = val + minVal;
```

"Multiply nested loops" would say O(k · n). **Wrong here.** The outer loop visits k slots. The inner loop runs `count[val]` times, and all the counts **add up to n** (we're putting n items back).

So it's **k + n**.

Whole thing: **O(n + k) time, O(k) space** (k = the range of values).

**Check:** k buckets whose sizes add up to n. Big-Oh?

lessons.title: Counting Recursive Calls
lessons.readme:
# Counting Recursive Calls

**The idea: count calls. How many calls does each call make (b), and how deep does it go (d)?**

| b | total calls | Big-Oh |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | d + 1 | O(d) |
| 2 | 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2ᵈ | O(2ᵈ) |
| 3 | 1 + 3 + 9 + … + 3ᵈ | O(3ᵈ) |

Then multiply by work per call.

**One call on n − 1** (the lecture's `sumArray`): b = 1, d = n → **O(n)** time and **O(n)** stack.

**Two calls on n − 1:**

```cpp
void g(int n) { if (n == 0) return; g(n - 1); g(n - 1); }
```

![call tree of g(3) with 15 calls](courses/diagrams/f94b018d-ada8-5e24-9ad2-21b6ae0b3dc4/calls.svg)

b = 2, d = n → **O(2ⁿ)**. g(3) makes 15 calls.

**Check:** three calls on n − 1. Big-Oh?

lessons.title: Recursion That Halves
lessons.readme:
# Recursion That Halves

**The idea: recursing on n/2 makes the depth log n, not n.**

**One call on n/2** (the midterm's fast power):

```cpp
long half = power(x, n / 2);     // one call, saved
return half * half;
```

b = 1, d = log n → **O(log n)**.

**Two calls on n/2:**

```cpp
return h(n / 2) + h(n / 2);
```

![call tree of h(8) with 15 calls](courses/diagrams/f2c9ddad-0607-5b34-b950-27b9a2401d4f/halves.svg)

b = 2, d = log n → 2^(log n) = **n** leaves → **O(n)**. Not O(2ⁿ).

That's why `power` saves `half` instead of calling itself twice.

**Check:** what is `h(n)`'s Big-Oh?

questions.question: The `power` function above makes **one** recursive call on n/2. Run time?

lessons.title: Best, Worst and Average Case
lessons.readme:
# Best, Worst and Average Case

**The idea: same size input can take different times. "Which case?" is a separate question from Big-Oh.**

- **Worst case:** the hardest input (key is last, or missing).
- **Average case:** expected time over typical inputs.
- **Best case:** the easiest input. **Not always O(1).**

Lab 3's `searchGrid`:

```cpp
for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
    for (int c = 0; c < cols; c++)
        if (grid[r][c] == target) { found = true; break; }
```

`break` only leaves the **inner** loop. Best case: the target is in column 0 of every row → one check per row → **O(rows)**.

Big-Oh can bound time, memory, network use, anything.

**Check:** best case of the grid loop?

lessons.title: Hidden Costs
lessons.readme:
# Hidden Costs

**The idea: a function call inside a loop costs its own Big-Oh, every time it runs.**

**A `size()` that walks the list:**

```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < list.size() / 2; i++) { ... }
```

If `size()` counts nodes (O(n)), it runs on **every** condition check: O(n) × n/2 = **O(n²)**.

**Passing by value** copies everything: O(n) before the function even starts. Use `const&` to only read.

**Library calls count:** `std::sort` is O(n log n). In a loop, multiply.

**Time and space are separate answers.** `countClashes`: O(n²) time, O(1) space.

**Check:** a loop calls a list-walking `size()` each pass. Big-Oh?

lessons.title: Big-Omega and Big-Theta
lessons.readme:
# Big-Omega and Big-Theta

**The idea: Big-Oh is a ceiling. Big-Omega is a floor. Big-Theta is both.**

- **Ω (Omega):** f(n) ≥ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀. A floor.
- **Θ (Theta):** f is O(g) **and** Ω(g). Pinned from both sides.

| statement | true? |
|---|---|
| 5n + 2 is O(n²) | yes (loose ceiling) |
| 5n + 2 is Ω(n) | yes |
| 5n + 2 is Θ(n) | yes |
| 5n + 2 is Θ(n²) | **no** |

These are separate from best/worst case. Pick the case first, then bound it.

The lecture's swap sort has no early exit, so even a sorted list takes n(n − 1)/2 steps: best case **Θ(n²)**.

**Check:** which statement is false?

lessons.title: When an Array Fills Up
lessons.readme:
# When an Array Fills Up

**The idea: a full growable array makes a bigger one and copies everything over. That one push costs O(n).**

Like moving to a bigger apartment: you carry every box over.

A **fixed** array just refuses: push stays O(1), with a hard limit.

A **growable** array:
1. Makes a bigger array.
2. Copies all n items.
3. Deletes the old one.

Two strategies for the new size:
- **Incremental:** add c slots.
- **Doubling:** double it.

![array growing from 1 to 2 to 4 to 8 slots, copying each time](courses/diagrams/7117a78f-2645-582f-aa37-439f07c41032/grow.svg)

So what does push cost? The professor's answer: **"it depends."** Fixed: O(1). Growable: O(n) worst case.

**Check:** what does one resizing push cost?

lessons.title: Doubling a Full Array
lessons.readme:
# Doubling a Full Array

**The idea: when the array is full, double it and copy. Count every copy.**

`GrowArray` starts with room for 1. It tracks `cap`, `n` (items), and `copies`.

When `push` finds it full:

1. **Allocate** twice the capacity.
2. **Copy** the n old items, adding 1 to `copies` each time.
3. **`delete[]`** the old array. Point `data` at the new one.

Then store the item and bump n.

8 pushes resize at 1, 2, 4: copies = 1 + 2 + 4 = 7.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `push(x)`. If the array is full, double its capacity: allocate, copy (counting each copy in `copies`), `delete[]` the old array, and update `data` and `cap`.
2. [ ] Store `x` at the end and update `n`.

Don't grow by a constant. The tests push 100,000 items and check the copy count.

lessons.title: Amortized Analysis
lessons.readme:
# Amortized Analysis

**The idea: one push can be expensive, but averaged over many pushes, doubling costs O(1) each.**

**Amortized time** = total time for n operations ÷ n.

Like a gym membership: one big payment, but per visit it's cheap.

**Doubling:** copies 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n ≈ 2n. Plus n stores. Total ≈ **3n** → **O(1)** per push.

**Add c each time:** copies c + 2c + 3c + … → about n²/c → **O(n)** per push.

![copies per resize: doubling makes 4 resizes, growing by 2 makes 7](courses/diagrams/a02a9429-3843-5ce1-89ad-fc2651fe132d/copies.svg)

With doubling, resizes get rarer as fast as they get bigger. That's why `vector::push_back` is O(1) amortized.

**Check:** amortized cost per push with doubling?

lessons.title: Analysis Review: Loops
lessons.readme:
# Analysis Review: Loops

**The idea: a checklist for every loop question.**

- List every input that can vary.
- Inner count fixed? **Multiply.** Depends on i? **Table + sum.**
- One after another? **Add.**
- Counter × or ÷ each pass? **log n.**
- Doubling outer, `j < i`? **2n − 1 → O(n).**
- `break` leaves only the inner loop.
- Inner counts add up to n? **O(n + k).**

Then simplify and write one sentence of justification.

**Check:** do all three on paper first.

lessons.title: Analysis Review: Proofs and Recursion
lessons.readme:
# Analysis Review: Proofs and Recursion

**The idea: a checklist for proofs and recursion.**

- **O:** f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for n ≥ n₀. Prove: pick c, solve for n₀.
- **Disprove:** suppose c exists, find an n that breaks it.
- **Ω** = floor. **Θ** = both.
- Case (best/worst/avg) is separate from O/Ω/Θ.
- Recursion: b calls, depth d. b = 1 → O(d). b ≥ 2 → O(bᵈ).
- Depth: n for `n − 1`, log n for `n / 2`. Stack space = depth.
- Doubling array: O(1) amortized. Adding c: O(n) amortized.

**Check:** do all three on paper first.

1. **Swapped pair.** Best and worst (or O and Ω) traded.

4. **Plain rule.** A loose bound is still a true bound.

lessons.title: Why Linked Lists?
lessons.readme:
# Why Linked Lists?

**The idea: a linked list is a chain of small boxes. Each box holds a value and an arrow to the next box.**

Like a scavenger hunt. Each clue tells you where the next clue is.

Adding a card to the top of an array deck shifts **every** card. A linked list drops that problem: each card is its own **node**, anywhere in memory.

```cpp
struct Node {
    int elt;      // the data
    Node* next;   // the next node, or nullptr at the end
};
```

![an array next to a linked list whose nodes sit at scattered addresses](courses/diagrams/233e412b-2d8e-5cdd-aac7-dac71095bbf0/array.svg)

The list is just one pointer, `head`, to the first node. The last node's `next` is `nullptr` (drawn ∅).

**Check:** how do you reach the fourth node?

questions.question: How do you reach the fourth node of a linked list?
answers: Jump to it with an index, as in an array
Start at the last node and step backward
Add 3 to the address stored in head
Start at head and follow next three times
questions.answer: Start at head and follow next three times

questions.question: True or false: the nodes of a linked list sit side by side in memory, the way array cells do.

# The List ADT

**The idea: an ADT says what operations do, not how they're built.**

**ADT** = abstract data type. Like a TV remote: you know "volume up" works. You don't care about the circuit inside.

The **List ADT** has operations like insert, remove and retrieve.

Two ways to build it:
- the array list from Lab 2
- the linked list from Lab 4

Same operations, different costs. This chapter compares them one by one.

> [!note]
> Lab 4's node is a template, `LinkedListNode<T>`. Here we use the plain `int` version from the midterm worksheet.

**Check:** what does the List ADT describe?

questions.question: The List ADT describes:
answers: How each node is laid out in memory
Which C++ class you must use
What the operations do, not how
questions.answer: What the operations do, not how

questions.question: Lab 2's array list and Lab 4's linked list both implement the List ADT. What do they share?
answers: The same Big O for every operation

# Nodes and Traversal

**The idea: to learn anything about a linked list, walk it node by node with a pointer called `cur`.**

```cpp
for (Node* cur = head; cur != nullptr; cur = cur->next) {
    // use cur->elt
}
```

![cur walks a three-node list and stops at nullptr](courses/diagrams/248da275-d60a-54e0-bf35-8683a1155840/walk.svg)

- `cur` is a **copy** of `head`. Moving it doesn't change the list.
- Empty list? `head` is `nullptr`, the loop runs zero times. Free.

Quiz 4 asked for `findValue` by hand. Points came off for:

> [!warning]
> - `ptr->next != nullptr` (skips the last node). Use `ptr != nullptr`.
> - Comparing `ptr == val`. Compare `ptr->elt == val`.
> - `return false` inside the loop. It goes **after** the loop.

> [!tip]
> Test on paper with: empty, one node, a few nodes.

# Insert at the Front

**The idea: new node points at the old head, then head moves to the new node. Three steps, nothing shifts.**

1. **Make** a new node.
2. **Link:** its `next` = the current `head`.
3. **Move** `head` to the new node.

![insertFront in three steps: allocate, link to head, move head](courses/diagrams/67504afa-916f-5f17-bb9c-d8d06f3896c9/steps.svg)

Empty list? Same steps work: the new node's `next` becomes `nullptr`.

In one line (`new Node{v, head}` fills `elt`, then `next`):

```cpp
head = new Node{v, head};
```

**Why `Node*& head`?** The function must change the **caller's** `head`. Without `&`, it changes a copy, and the new node leaks.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `insertFront(head, v)` so a new node holding `v` becomes the first node. It must work on an empty list, and it must keep every existing node (don't copy them).

lessons.readme:
# Insert at the Front Big O

**The idea: inserting at the front is O(1). Three cards or three million, same work.**

One `new`, two pointer writes. Nothing depends on length.

| | array list | linked list |
|---|---|---|
| insertFront | O(n): shift everything | **O(1)** |

That's the main reason to pick a linked list.

**Side effect for tracing:** each new node goes in front, so inserting at the front **reverses** the order:

```
insertFront 1, 2, 3   →   head → 3 → 2 → 1 → ∅
```

**Check:** trace the loop below.

So the list can't be changed

lessons.title: Remove from the Front
lessons.readme:
# Remove from the Front

**The idea: save the front node, move head forward, then delete the saved node. In that order.**

1. **Save:** `Node* tmp = head;`
2. **Move:** `head = head->next;`
3. **Delete:** `delete tmp;`

![removeFront: save tmp, move head, delete tmp](courses/diagrams/eca44f54-96d1-5db1-827f-96c15e9e8ef7/steps.svg)

Wrong orders:
- `head = head->next;` alone: old front **leaks**.
- `delete tmp;` then `head = head->next;`: reads **freed memory**.
- `head = head->next; delete head;`: deletes the **wrong** node.

**Rule:** grab everything you need from a node **before** deleting it.

Empty list? There's nothing to remove. Check first.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `removeFront(head)`. If the list is empty, return `false` and change nothing.
2. [ ] Otherwise remove the first node, `delete` it, and return `true`. A one-node list ends up with `head == nullptr`.

The tests run with a leak checker.

| removeFront | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) |

# Insert at the Back

**The idea: with only a head pointer, walk to the last node, then link the new one after it.**

1. Start `cur` at `head`.
2. Follow `next` until `cur->next == nullptr`. Now `cur` is the last node.
3. Link the new node after it.

![insertBack: walk cur to the last node, then link the new node](courses/diagrams/ceaabaae-b4ae-508b-965e-50b065987ad0/steps.svg)

Stop when `cur->next` is null, **not** `cur`. Otherwise you walk off the end with nothing to link to.

Empty list? There's no last node. Handle it first:

```cpp
if (head == nullptr) { head = n; return; }
```

The walk visits every node: **O(n)**.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `insertBack(head, v)`. If the list is empty, the new node becomes `head`.
2. [ ] Otherwise walk to the last node and link the new node after it.
